content.text:
**Ответ: кандидат 0.** Я считал в уме и грубо, поэтому разницы ниже — оценки порядка величины, а не точные цифры.

**Чем отличаются планы.** Кандидат 0 заказывает ровно прогноз на день прихода: в день t товара 0 — mu[t+4], товара 1 — mu[t+2]. Остальные планы — это то же самое с множителем:
- кандидат 5 — ×0,9;
- кандидат 4 — ×1,1;
- кандидат 1 — ×1,3;
- кандидат 3 — товар 0 ×1,0, товар 1 ×1,2;
- кандидаты 6 и 7 — около ×1,2 (у кандидата 6 последние заказы возвращаются к прогнозу);
- кандидат 2 — заказы на два дня сразу через день, около ×1,1.

**Общие потери.** В первые дни нехватка одинакова у всех: товара 0 до дня 4 есть только 26 при спросе около 69, товара 1 в дни 0–1 — 40 при спросе около 64. На сравнение это не влияет.

**Как сравнивал.** Остатки переходят на следующий день, поэтому недопродажа за весь срок — это наибольший накопленный разрыв между спросом и поставками. Средний спрос примерно на 4,6 % выше прогноза. Отсюда:
- **Товар 1** (каждая потерянная единица стоит 18 + 7 = 25). При ×1,0 теряется около 65 ед. Переход на ×1,1 снижает потери примерно до 20 ед., то есть экономит около 1 100. Но он стоит около 1 070 на закупку плюс около 500 хранения растущего запаса. Значит, ×1,0 выгоднее ×1,1. Переход с ×0,9 на ×1,0 экономит около 2 100 потерь при росте закупки примерно на 1 070, поэтому ×0,9 хуже.
- **Товар 0** (единица стоит 21). Переход с ×1,0 на ×1,1 экономит около 570, а стоит около 595 на закупку плюс около 150 хранения. Снова ×1,0 немного выгоднее.
- **При ×1,2 и ×1,3** (кандидаты 1, 6, 7) лишний запас растёт примерно на 8 ед. в день. К середине месяца склад упирается в предел 176 единиц, и оплаченный товар 1 пропадает при приходе. К этому добавляются хранение и списания.
- **Кандидат 2** экономит около 224 на сборах за заказ: 14 дней с заказом вместо 28. Но хранение половины партии лишний день обходится примерно в 390, плюс у него те же потери от ×1,1.
- **Кандидат 3** теряет на перезаказе товара 1 (×1,2) больше 1 000.

**Устойчивость.** При ×1,0 запас не копится, поэтому план не упирается в склад и почти не теряет на списаниях. Нехватка частично гасится остатками прошлых дней. Денег хватает: дневные закупки около 600 покрываются выручкой.

Наибольший ожидаемый итог у кандидата 0. Кандидат 4 отстаёт примерно на 600, остальные — сильнее.

I picked **candidate 0**. It orders exactly the forecast, shifted by each item's lead time: for item 0 it orders day t+4's forecast, for item 1 day t+2's. The other candidates are the same plan scaled by about 0.9, 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3, and candidate 2 also orders every other day.

**Same for every plan.** The starting stock (26 of item 0, 40 of item 1) runs out within the first days, before the first orders arrive. The shortfall penalties in those days are identical for all candidates, so I left them out.

**How I compared them.** The plans never react to actual demand, so stock on hand behaves like a random walk that resets to zero when stock runs out. Each day it moves by the amount delivered minus demand. Rewriting the profit with this in mind:
- Item 0: profit ≈ 10·(units bought) − 21·(units left at the end or expired) − storage cost.
- Item 1: profit ≈ 14·(units bought) − 25·(units left at the end or expired) − storage cost.

I estimated the expected leftover with the formula for the maximum of a random walk with drift. Average demand is 1.046 × forecast. Daily spread is about 32 % of the forecast, which gives about 35 units over the whole period for item 0 and about 61 for item 1.

**Item 0** (expected profit by scale factor):

| Scale | Expected leftover | Storage | Profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | ~8 | ~60 | ~4640 |
| 1.0 | ~18 | ~125 | ~4910 |
| 1.1 | ~46 | ~260 | ~4730 |
| 1.2 | ~91 | ~470 | ~4110 |

**Item 1:**

| Scale | Expected leftover | Profit |
|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | ~13 | ~11720 |
| 1.0 | ~31 | ~12440 |
| 1.1 | ~81 | ~12160 |
| 1.2 | ~162 | ~10900, before losses from expiry |

At a scale of 1.0, one extra unit still earns a little, about +1. By 1.1 it already loses about −6. The best scale is therefore about 1.02, so ordering the forecast is closer to it than any other candidate.

**Why the others lose:**
- **Candidates 1, 6, 7 (scale about 1.2–1.3):** leftovers and storage grow too much. Candidate 6 only cuts back to the forecast for the last few orders, which doesn't save it.
- **Candidate 3:** item 0 is at the forecast, but item 1 is at about 1.2, which costs roughly 1500 on item 1.
- **Candidate 4 (1.1):** about 450 less than candidate 0.
- **Candidate 5 (0.9):** shortage penalties cost about 1000 more.
- **Candidate 2:** it is also at about 1.1. Ordering every other day saves about 13 × 16 ≈ 208 in order fees. But it holds one day's demand of both items overnight every other day, which costs about 420 in storage, and large deliveries risk hitting the 176-unit limit.

**Randomness.** Being 10 % above the forecast is almost free when demand comes in high but costs a lot when it comes in low. The open-loop plans can't correct, so excess just piles up. That makes the forecast plan the steadiest of the eight too.

**Choice: candidate 0.** It orders exactly the forecast, about 1.0×, for both products. I worked this out with rough math in my head, not by simulating, and candidate 4 (about 1.1×) comes out close behind.

**What the plans are.** Every plan is the forecast for the arrival day (day t + L) multiplied by a constant:

| Candidate | Product 0 | Product 1 | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1.0 | 1.0 | |
| 1 | 1.3 | 1.3 | |
| 2 | 1.1 | 1.1 | orders every other day, double quantity |
| 3 | 1.0 | 1.2 | |
| 4 | 1.1 | 1.1 | |
| 5 | 0.9 | 0.9 | |
| 6 | 1.2 | 1.2 | drops to 1.0 for the last orders |
| 7 | 1.2 | 1.2 | |

All plans stop ordering in time, so nothing is paid for that would arrive after day 29.

**Losses every plan shares.**
- **Product 0:** the starting 26 units cover only day 0. Orders first arrive on day 4, so about 43 units are short on days 1–3 whatever the plan.
- **Product 1:** the starting 40 units leave a shortfall of about 24 units on day 1.

**Main finding.** Unsold stock carries over to the next day, and shelf life (7 days and 5 days) almost never runs out at these stock levels. So stock behaves like a running balance of arrivals minus demand that can't go below zero. Shortages come from the dips in that balance, and anything left over at the end is lost money.

**Product 0 (days 4–29).** Average demand is about 566 units, with a spread of about ±34 over the period.

| Rate | Bought | Expected shortage | Leftover at end | Holding |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 541 | ≈38 | ≈13 | ≈105 |
| 1.1 | 595 | ≈13 | ≈42 | ≈230 |
| 0.9 | — | ≈84 | — | — |

Each extra unit costs 11 to buy. Each shortage costs 21 (15 lost sale plus the 6 penalty). On that basis 1.0 beats 1.1 by about 190, and 0.9 is clearly worse.

**Product 1 (days 2–29).** Average demand is about 1015 units, with a spread of about ±60.

| Rate | Bought | Expected shortage | Holding |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 970 | ≈68 | ≈250 |
| 1.1 | 1067 | ≈23 | ≈700 |

Each shortage costs 25 (18 lost sale plus the 7 penalty). Here 1.0 beats 1.1 by about 390. At 1.2 and 1.3, stock piles up, so holding costs, overflow past the 176-unit warehouse limit and the worthless leftover at the end all grow.

**Ranking.**
- **Candidate 0 vs 4:** 0 comes out about 500–600 ahead.
- **Candidate 3:** extra product-1 stock it can't sell. Worse than 0.
- **Candidates 6 and 7:** both overstock; 6 is slightly better because of its smaller final orders.
- **Candidate 1:** overstocks the most.
- **Candidate 5:** too many shortages.
- **Candidate 2:** ordering every other day saves about 208 in ordering fees but adds about 400 in holding, on top of candidate 4's costs.

**How sure I am.** If actual demand runs high, candidate 4 wins. Its gap behind candidate 0 is moderate, and my estimates of shortages and holding are approximate. That's why my confidence that candidate 0 is really the best is only about 0.5.

**Choice: candidate 0.** I worked this out by hand with rough approximations, not a simulation. The ranking is fairly robust, but the cost figures below are only estimates.

**What the candidates are.** Each plan orders the forecast of the day the order will arrive (day t + 4 for product 0, day t + 2 for product 1), times a scaling factor:
- Candidate 0 uses the forecast as is (×1.0).
- Candidate 5 is ×0.9, candidate 4 is ×1.1, candidates 7 and 6 are ×1.2, and candidate 1 is ×1.3. Candidate 6 drops back to the plain forecast in its last orders.
- Candidate 3 uses ×1.0 for product 0 and ×1.2 for product 1.
- Candidate 2 orders about ×1.1 in two-day batches.

The plan is fixed and nothing adjusts to actual demand. The start is the same for everyone: product 1 runs short on days 0–1 and product 0 on days 0–3, before the first orders arrive.

**What a shortage or a leftover costs.**
- Product 1: a missed sale costs 7 of margin plus a 7 penalty, so 14. A unit left over at the end is a wasted 11 purchase. Total cost ≈ 25·(total shortage) + 11·(cumulative over-ordering) + holding.
- Product 0: the same logic gives ≈ 21·(total shortage) + 11·(cumulative over-ordering) + holding.

**Why over-ordering doesn't pay.** With a fixed plan, any surplus just builds up over the month. There is no point where the plan corrects, and whatever is left on day 29 is a total loss. Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast, so:
- At ×1.0 there is a small daily deficit: about −1.5 units/day for product 1 and −0.9 for product 0.
- At ×1.1 there is a surplus of about +1.7 and +1.0.
- At ×1.2 the surplus is about +4.7 for product 1, which comes to roughly 130 surplus units by the end of the month.

**Rough cost estimates** (I treated the stock level as a random walk that can't go below zero):
- Product 1: ×1.0 ≈ 1,420; ordering exactly the average demand ≈ 1,400; ×1.1 ≈ 1,660; ×0.9 ≈ 2,080; ×1.2 ≈ 2,800 or more, mostly from wasted leftovers and holding.
- Product 0: ×1.0 ≈ 630; ×1.1 ≈ 810.

**Other candidates.**
- Candidate 2 saves about 13 order fees (about 208), but holding each batch an extra night costs about 14 per day across both products. That costs more than it saves.
- Candidates 1, 6, 7 and 3 (for product 1) over-order and lose to waste and holding. Cutting back at the end only partly helps candidate 6.
- Candidate 5 runs short too often.

Candidate 0 sits closest to the best level for both products and has the lowest expected cost. Candidate 4 comes second, about 400 behind.
